why_this_tool: etcd is a small single-binary Raft store that runs as a three-member cluster on a laptop, so linearizable reads, revisions, quorum loss, leases and locks can all be observed directly instead of only read about.
alternatives: ZooKeeper offers the same coordination primitives through ephemeral znodes and its own Zab protocol, with a heavier JVM footprint; Consul bundles a Raft key-value store with service discovery and health checks; CockroachDB and Spanner put consensus under full SQL transactions with serializable isolation; PostgreSQL gives rich isolation levels on a single primary without built-in consensus.

setup.do: Install the etcd server and the etcdctl client from a release archive and confirm both report the same version.
setup.done_when: Asking etcd and etcdctl for their version prints matching v3 version numbers.
setup.why: Every later item is driven through etcdctl against a local server, and the reading guide lists exactly what must be in place first.

setup.do: Start the three-member demo etcd cluster on your laptop, each member with its own name, data directory and ports.
setup.done_when: The member list shows three started members and endpoint status shows exactly one leader.

setup.why: Consensus and quorum only become visible with several members; a single node hides every interesting failure.

setup.do: Open the latest documentation landing page and confirm it matches the version you installed.
setup.done_when: The version shown in the docs matches the version printed by your etcd binary.
setup.why: Flags and behaviour differ between minor versions, so following the wrong version of the docs wastes time.

steps.do: Write your first key and value to the cluster with etcdctl put.
steps.done_when: The client prints OK and the same key can be written again with a new value.
steps.why: A write is the smallest operation that must go through the Raft leader and be accepted by a majority before it is acknowledged.

steps.do: Read the key back, then read a whole key prefix, and print one result in JSON output so the header and key metadata are visible.
steps.done_when: You can point at the cluster revision, the create revision, the mod revision and the version of your key in the output.
steps.why: The core object model of etcd is a flat key space where every key carries a create revision, a mod revision and a version, all under one cluster-wide revision counter.

steps.do: Write the same key several more times, then read it at an older revision while a second terminal keeps writing new values.
steps.done_when: A read pinned to an old revision keeps returning the old value while an unpinned read returns the newest one.
steps.why: This is the subtopic on transactions and isolation levels: multi-version storage lets a reader see one consistent snapshot, which is the mechanism behind snapshot and serializable isolation and behind compare-and-swap on a revision.

steps.do: Compare a linearizable read with a serializable read of one key, sending each to a single follower endpoint.
steps.done_when: You can state which read mode is the default, which one is faster, and which one could return an old value.
steps.why: This is the consistency-model subtopic: a linearizable read is confirmed through the quorum and never goes back in time, while a serializable read is answered from the local member and may be stale, which is the etcd version of the strong-to-eventual spectrum.

steps.do: Stop one member of the demo cluster and write a key, then stop a second member and try both a write and the two read modes.
steps.done_when: With two members up the write succeeds, with one member up the write and the linearizable read time out and the serializable read still returns, and restarting a member restores writes.

source.title: How to Set Up a Demo etcd Cluster | etcd

steps.why: This is the consensus, quorums and Raft subtopic: two of three members form a majority and keep working, one of three cannot commit anything, and only the local serializable read still answers.

steps.do: Create a lease with a short time to live, attach a key to it, and let it expire without keeping it alive.
steps.done_when: The key is readable while the lease lives and disappears on its own after the time to live passes.
steps.why: A lease is a time-bounded promise from the cluster; it is how a crashed client loses its claims without anyone cleaning up by hand.

steps.do: Create a named lock in one terminal and try to acquire the same lock name from a second terminal.
steps.done_when: The second terminal blocks until the first releases the lock, then prints its own lock key.
steps.why: A distributed lock in etcd is a leased key plus an ordering by revision, so seeing the second client wait shows what the store actually guarantees.

steps.do: Configure the lock with a short session time to live, kill the holder process abruptly, and time how long the waiter takes to get the lock.
steps.done_when: The waiter acquires the lock roughly one time to live after the kill, and you can explain why a paused holder is dangerous in that window.
steps.why: The lock is only as safe as its lease: a paused or dead holder keeps the lock until the lease runs out, and a paused holder may still believe it owns it afterwards.

steps.do: Query the ownership key that the lock command printed, in JSON output, and record its create revision as a fencing token for two successive holders.
steps.done_when: The second holder has a strictly higher create revision than the first, and you can describe the check the protected resource must perform.
steps.why: This completes the leases, locks and fencing subtopic: a downstream resource that rejects any request carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen is what makes a lease-based lock safe.

steps.do: Reproduce the storage memory usage benchmark at laptop scale, writing down your own testing environment in the same form the page uses and loading a much smaller number of keys.
steps.done_when: You have a short note with your environment, key count and measured memory that a colleague could rerun and compare with the published table.
steps.why: A result that names its machine, version and data shape can be rerun by anyone, and it shows how every key and revision costs memory in the index.

steps.do: Run a rolling upgrade of the three-member cluster, replacing one member binary at a time while a client keeps writing.
steps.done_when: All three members report the new version, the cluster version has moved up, and the writing client saw no lost acknowledged writes.

source.title: Upgrading etcd clusters and applications | etcd

steps.why: Production clusters are changed while serving traffic, and a rolling change only works because the quorum survives one member being down.

steps.do: Run the documented downgrade procedure on the same cluster to return it to the previous minor version, checking health after every member.
steps.done_when: Every member reports the earlier version, endpoint health is green on all three, and the keys written before the downgrade are still readable.

source.title: Downgrading etcd clusters and applications | etcd

steps.why: A production-like setup needs a tested way back, and downgrading exercises the same quorum and version-agreement rules under more constraints.
